title: How to write SOPs for support teams and AI workflows | Pylon
summary: Learn how to write SOPs for support teams with clear steps, triggers, decisions, and escalations. Then learn how to turn SOPs into reusable Pylon Skills.
body_markdown:
It’s natural for people to develop their own ways of getting things done. But when everyone on a support team approaches the same tasks differently, it’s impossible to deliver consistent support. As teams grow, those differences become more noticeable and can create unnecessary back-and-forth or easily avoidable miscommunication.


With standard operating procedures (SOPs), teams can establish a shared approach to common, repeatable support tasks.


This guide breaks down what SOPs are and provides a template for how to write SOPs. We’ll also explore why gaps can remain in some procedures, and how to turn finished SOPs into reusable Pylon Skills.


## What’s an SOP?


Ask AI in Pylon


A standard operating procedure is a documented, step-by-step process for completing a task. It gives team members clear instructions to follow consistently, so everyone can handle requests and tickets the same way. Over time, regular use with slight refinement[improves customer support processes](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/customer-service-process-improvement) .


SOPs outline the overall process, including who’s responsible for each step and when to escalate or hand off a task. SOPs are often the most useful for recurring tasks with a definable process targeting a clear outcome, going into greater detail about how to perform a specific action within that process.


Here are a few common examples:


- **Integration troubleshooting.** Walk agents through diagnostic checks and help them determine when an issue requires further escalation.
- **Bug escalations to dev teams.** Establish what information developers need before taking over a ticket.
- **Incident updates for affected accounts.** Set expectations for communicating with accounts impacted by a bug or outage.
- **Handoffs to post-sales teams after a deal closes.** Standardize how sales teams transfer account details and customer requirements to those responsible for onboarding.


Having SOPs should be standard practice for frequently occurring, repeatable tasks. They’re also valuable for[scaling customer support tasks](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/scaling-customer-support) that require a clear process to avoid mistakes or miscommunications.


## Why support SOPs break down


When you’re familiar with a process, it’s easy to overlook simple details that someone else might need explained. This often carries over into writing SOPs, where instructions can leave too much room for assumptions.


Some common failure points include:


- **Unclear decision points.** The SOP doesn’t explain when to take one action over another.
- **Missing triggers.** The SOP describes a process without identifying the events or requests that should initiate it.
- **Undefined escalation paths.** Team members don’t know who to contact when they can’t resolve a problem.
- **Outdated instructions.** The SOP no longer reflects revisions to tools or internal processes and procedures.
- **Poor accessibility.** Documentation is scattered across different tools or gets lost in a[knowledge base](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/knowledge-base-articles-what-they-are-how-to-make-them-effective) .


These gaps become much more apparent when AI agents follow the same procedures. An experienced support rep can draw from previous experience to fill in missing details, but an AI agent relies on the instructions and context available. Unclear steps lead to errors and incomplete workflows.


## How to write an SOP in 6 steps


Agent runbook in Pylon


When writing an SOP, assume the person following it knows nothing about the task. Every step should be so clear that a new hire can complete the task without additional guidance.


Here’s how to write standard operating procedures in six simple steps.


### 1. Choose one repeatable process


Begin with a straightforward, high-volume task your team handles regularly; SOPs work best when they have a clear trigger and outcome.


In this example, we’ll document how to troubleshoot a failed CRM data sync.


### 2. Map the workflow from trigger to outcome


Gather information from support team members who handle failed CRM data syncs and observe how they troubleshoot them. Outline the process, including what information they need, which tools to use, and how to know the issue has been resolved.


### 3. Fill in the core SOP fields


Jot down basic information about the procedure. Give your SOP a clear title, define the scope, and identify roles and responsibilities for the process.


Here’s a procedure template we’ll use to document how to troubleshoot a failed CRM data sync:


SOP field What to write


Title Troubleshooting failed CRM data syncs


Purpose Identify and resolve data synchronization errors between a customer’s CRM and Pylon software.


Scope


Troubleshoot failed data syncs between a CRM integration connected to Pylon.


Excludes initial setup, configuration changes, and unrelated integration errors.


Expected outcome Data syncing resumes and the fix is verified, or the issue escalates with supporting evidence.


Owner Assign the individual responsible for the SOP and their role or title.


Trigger A customer reports missing CRM data, delayed updates, or a sync error.


Prerequisites Access to the customer’s integration status and error logs.


Tools Integration dashboard, internal knowledge base, CRM admin console.


Review and approval The technical support manager reviews the SOP every six months, or whenever CRM integration or troubleshooting processes change.


### 4. Write one action per step


Break down the procedure into numbered steps. Each should begin with an active action verb. Avoid vague instructions like “investigate the sync failure.” Instead, specify where to find the information and what to check.


For instance, the first step might be “Open the integration dashboard and locate the most recent failed CRM sync.” Include screenshots or links to your knowledge base when additional context may be useful.


### 5. Spell out decision points and escalations


Explain when to take a specific action over another. If the CRM connection shows expired credentials, for example, direct the agent to reauthorization instructions. For connections that are active, but syncing still fails, explain how to escalate to engineering. Specify error logs or other context the next team member will need.


### 6. Test, review, and schedule updates


Give the finished SOP to someone unfamiliar with the troubleshooting process and ask them to follow it without further assistance. Use their feedback to clarify any confusing instructions, and repeat testing.


Have the appropriate manager approve the finished SOP before putting it into use. Review it whenever integration tools or procedures change, and set a regular review cadence to scan for outdated information.


## How to turn SOPs into Pylon Skills


When reps use[AI customer support](https://usepylon.com/blog/ai-for-customer-support) to investigate tickets, they often write their own prompts to tell the agent what to do. When someone develops a particularly useful set of instructions, their colleagues may never see it, hindering[improvements to customer support quality](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/improve-customer-support-quality) . Pylon’s Skills makes those instructions reusable across the entire team.


First, create a Skill:


- **Begin with an existing SOP.** Paste your documented procedure into a new Skill on Pylon’s Skills page, or share it with Pylon’s Assist Agent and ask the agent to turn it into a Skill.
- **Build from a real issue.** Work through an actual support request with Assist Agent, then ask the agent to convert it into a reusable Skill.
- **Import existing Skills.** Upload skill files from other AI tools.


Then, configure and test your Skill:


- **Define the trigger.** Describe when the Skill should run, beginning with specific qualifying and framing language while naming symptoms of relevant situations.
- **Choose the agent.** An Assist Agent Skill produces an internal briefing for the team, while a Support Agent Skill produces a reply for the customer.
- **Keep the scope narrow.** Create one Skill per unique situation instead of trying to have one Skill cover all scenarios.
- **Specify the output.** Define what the Skill should produce, like a draft reply, an internal summary, or an escalation.
- **Check tool access.** Use Connectors to give the Skill access to necessary tools.
- **Backtest the Skill.** Test the Skill against past issues to identify gaps before deployment.


Once a Skill is ready, there are several ways it can work. Support reps can run it manually using a /command in Assist Agent, while Pylon Automations can run Skills on incoming issues before the team picks it up. The Support Agent can also run Skills independently when handling customer requests.


Over time, Pylon suggests improvements based on how a Skill performs. Your team can review those recommendations and approve changes.

## FAQ


### How detailed should an SOP be?


An SOP should provide enough detail for someone unfamiliar with the task to complete it without assistance. Include clear directions, decision points, and screenshots or links when additional guidance may be useful.


### What’s excluded from an SOP?


An SOP should exclude tasks and procedures outside its defined scope. Reference separate documentation when related processes require additional instructions.


### Who should be involved in writing and reviewing an SOP?


Team members who regularly perform the task should help write the SOP. A team lead or other expert should review it for accuracy. Assign an owner with a clear role and responsibility to maintain the document and approve revisions.


### How do you create an SOP manual?


Organize related SOPs in a shared knowledge base with a table of contents for easy navigation. Use consistent SOP formats, clear titles, and version numbers so employees can find the latest instructions.
